identity.title: Sensory level with hyperreflexia / extensor plantar (Babinski) below the level

technique.how: Test pinprick and light touch moving upward from the feet on both sides (front and back) to find the dermatome where sensation becomes normal; confirm with temperature. Then test deep tendon reflexes in arms and legs, clonus, and the plantar response by stroking the lateral sole from heel toward the toes with a blunt object; the great toe extending upward (Babinski) is abnormal.
technique.prerequisites: Cooperative patient; interpret the plantar response only when the patient is relaxed and the stimulus is firm but not painful. Ask about bowel/bladder function and check a post-void residual.
technique.contraindications: None; avoid moving an unstable spine (trauma) beyond log-roll.

interpretation.positive_finding: A dermatomal sensory level with bilateral hyperreflexia, clonus or extensor plantars below it localizes a myelopathy and, with back pain or known cancer, suggests cord compression requiring emergency MRI and dexamethasone/oncology-spine referral.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of a sensory level or UMN signs does not exclude cord compression: reflexes may be absent early (spinal shock) and the Babinski sign has fair reliability (kappa 0.30) and only 56% agreement with known UMN weakness.
interpretation.pitfalls: Areflexia with ascending weakness favours GBS, but acute cord lesions can also be areflexic initially; a bilateral or cervical sensory level with hemibody signs may be misread as stroke. Withdrawal responses mimic Babinski; foot-tapping speed may be a more reliable UMN sign.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: emergency whole-spine MRI, steroids if malignancy suspected, spinal/oncology referral. Negative: does not exclude compression in cancer patients with new back pain - still image.

sources.citation: Emergency neurological life support: spinal cord compression (SCC). Neurocrit Care. 2012;17 Suppl 1:S96-S101.
Miller TM, Johnston SC. Should the Babinski sign be part of the routine neurologic examination? Neurology. 2005;65(8):1165-1168.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use a normal exam to withhold urgent MRI in a patient with known malignancy and new/progressive back pain or bladder symptoms; the sensory level and Babinski are insensitive early signs.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Suspected cord compression is time-critical - neurological outcome depends on ambulatory status at treatment; image and treat within hours, not days.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Babinski sign inter-rater reliability was fair (kappa 0.30) and accuracy 56% among 10 physicians examining 10 subjects, with no difference between neurologists and non-specialists; foot tapping had kappa 0.73 and 85% agreement (Miller & Johnston 2005). No reliability data for sensory level identified.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study reporting sensitivity/specificity of a sensory level or of UMN signs for spinal cord compression was found (searches: RCE title search, 'metastatic spinal cord compression clinical signs sensitivity sensory level'). The sign is supported by consensus protocols (ENLS spinal cord compression, PMID 22956117, cited as guideline). Miller & Johnston 2005 provides reliability/accuracy data for the Babinski sign (kappa 0.30; 56% agreement with known UMN weakness) from the abstract, which are not sens/spec against a reference standard and are therefore recorded in interobserver_note rather than as an estimate. NICE NG234 could not be retrieved and is not cited.
